title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene (603415) on chromosome 2q24.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD) is a rare autosomal dominant pain disorder linked to a mutation in the SCN9A gene
checks.explanation: The abstract links PEPD to SCN9A mutation with autosomal dominant inheritance, and the patient's mutation is described as heterozygous.

checks.claim: The SCN9A gene is located on chromosome 2q24.
checks.evidence_quote: mutational analysis of the candidate gene SCN9A, which encodes hNa(v)1.7
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature that restates the gene the paper names; the abstract itself does not give 2q24.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is an autosomal dominant neuropathic pain disorder that starts in the neonatal period or infancy and lasts throughout life. It is marked by attacks of severe burning pain in the rectal, ocular, and submandibular areas. The attacks come with autonomic signs such as skin flushing, often in a harlequin pattern. Attacks can be set off by defecation, cold wind, eating, or emotion. In infants, attacks may include tonic nonepileptic episodes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole. The disorder was formerly called familial rectal pain syndrome.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is an autosomal dominant neuropathic pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: is an inherited condition characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing
checks.explanation: The abstract says only 'inherited condition'. Autosomal dominant inheritance and the term neuropathic are not stated.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder starts in the neonatal period or infancy and persists throughout life.
checks.evidence_quote: The onset of the disorder is in the neonatal period or infancy and persists throughout life.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is characterized by attacks of severe burning pain in the rectal, ocular, and submandibular areas.
checks.evidence_quote: attacks of excruciating deep burning pain often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas, but also diffuse

checks.evidence_quote: a familial autonomic disorder related to proctalgia fugaz

checks.evidence_quote: Attacks are triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2006) proposed the name 'paroxysmal extreme pain disorder' in place of 'familial rectal pain syndrome.' Their reason was that the pain is not limited to the rectum and also affects the eye and jaw areas.

checks.evidence_quote: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD), previously known as familial rectal pain (FRP, or OMIM 167400)
checks.explanation: The abstract uses the new name and gives the old one, but does not explicitly say the authors proposed the change.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2006) based the renaming on the fact that the pain of this disorder is not confined to the rectum but also involves the eye and jaw areas.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing
checks.explanation: Pain at sites other than the rectum is described, but the abstract does not give this as the reason for renaming.

paragraphs.text: Hayden and Grossman (1959) described a family in which affected members, across several generations, had attacks of pain in the rectum, eyes, and submandibular region together with flushing.

checks.explanation: The title confirms a family with rectal, ocular and submaxillary pain. It does not say that several generations were affected.

checks.claim: In the family described by Hayden and Grossman (1959), the pain attacks were accompanied by flushing.
checks.explanation: Only the title was supplied; it does not mention flushing, just an 'autonomic disorder'.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) gave a detailed clinical description of affected members from a series of families. In the neonatal period and infancy, the main features were autonomic: skin flushing, harlequin color change, and tonic attacks. Some infants also had syncope with bradycardia and occasional asystole. Excruciating rectal pain followed, typically triggered by defecation. Later in life, ocular and submandibular pain became more prominent, triggered by cold or eating. Carbamazepine helped some patients, at least in part.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2007) gave a detailed clinical description of affected members from a series of families with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Seventy-seven individuals from 15 families were identified.

checks.claim: In the families studied by Fertleman et al. (2007), the main features in the neonatal period and infancy were autonomic: skin flushing, harlequin color change, and tonic attacks.
checks.evidence_quote: Autonomic manifestations predominate initially, with skin flushing in all and harlequin color change and tonic attacks in most.

checks.claim: In the families studied by Fertleman et al. (2007), some infants had syncope with bradycardia and occasional asystole.
checks.evidence_quote: Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole are common.
checks.explanation: Abstract says syncopes are common but does not explicitly restrict them to infants.

checks.claim: In the families studied by Fertleman et al. (2007), the infantile autonomic features were followed by excruciating rectal pain, typically triggered by defecation.
checks.evidence_quote: Later, the disorder is characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas
checks.explanation: Rectal pain follows the infantile autonomic phase, but the abstract does not specifically tie rectal pain to defecation as its typical trigger.

checks.claim: In the families studied by Fertleman et al. (2007), ocular and submandibular pain became more prominent later in life, triggered by cold or eating.
checks.evidence_quote: Attacks are triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion.
checks.explanation: Ocular/jaw pain and cold/eating triggers are mentioned, but the abstract does not state that ocular/submandibular pain becomes more prominent later in life.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2007) found that carbamazepine was at least partially effective in some patients with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Carbamazepine is effective in almost all who try it, but the response is often incomplete.
checks.explanation: Paper says effective in almost all who try it (often incompletely), more than 'some patients'.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, as seen in the multigenerational families reported by Hayden and Grossman (1959) and Fertleman et al. (2006).

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
checks.evidence_quote: is an inherited condition
checks.explanation: The abstract does not specify autosomal dominant inheritance.

checks.claim: Hayden and Grossman (1959) reported a multigenerational family consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance of paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: a familial autonomic disorder related to proctalgia fugaz: report of a family.
checks.explanation: The title confirms a family report. Multiple generations and a dominant pattern are not in the title.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2006) reported multigenerational families consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance of paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: identified eight missense mutations in 11 families and 2 sporadic cases
checks.explanation: Families are reported, but the abstract does not describe them as multigenerational or state the inheritance pattern.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2006) identified heterozygous missense mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7, in families with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder. The mutations included I1461T and T1464I, which lie in the inactivation gate motif of the domain III-IV linker, and M1627K. Expressed in cells, the mutant channels showed impaired fast inactivation and a persistent sodium current. This differs from the hyperpolarizing shift in activation seen with SCN9A mutations that cause primary erythromelalgia.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2006) identified heterozygous missense mutations in the SCN9A gene in families with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: identified eight missense mutations in 11 families and 2 sporadic cases
checks.explanation: Zygosity (heterozygous) is not stated in the abstract.

checks.evidence_quote: the candidate gene SCN9A, which encodes hNa(v)1.7
checks.explanation: The abstract states that SCN9A encodes Nav1.7.

checks.claim: The SCN9A mutations identified by Fertleman et al. (2006) in paroxysmal extreme pain disorder included I1461T, T1464I, and M1627K.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not name any specific mutation; that detail would be in the full text.

checks.claim: The SCN9A I1461T and T1464I mutations lie in the inactivation gate motif of the domain III-IV linker.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not describe the location of specific mutations or the inactivation gate motif.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2006) found that the mutant SCN9A channels associated with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, when expressed in cells, showed impaired fast inactivation.
checks.evidence_quote: Functional analysis in vitro of three of these mutant Na(v)1.7 channels revealed a reduction in fast inactivation
checks.explanation: The abstract states reduced fast inactivation in the mutant channels.

checks.claim: Fertleman et al. (2006) found that the mutant SCN9A channels associated with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, when expressed in cells, produced a persistent sodium current.
checks.evidence_quote: revealed a reduction in fast inactivation, leading to persistent sodium current
checks.explanation: The abstract states the mutants produce a persistent sodium current.

checks.claim: The functional defect of SCN9A mutations in paroxysmal extreme pain disorder differs from the hyperpolarizing shift in activation seen with SCN9A mutations that cause primary erythromelalgia.
checks.evidence_quote: Other mutations in SCN9A associated with more negative activation thresholds are known to cause primary erythermalgia (PE).
checks.explanation: A more negative activation threshold is the same thing as a hyperpolarizing shift, and the abstract contrasts it with the PEPD defect.

paragraphs.text: Jarecki et al. (2010) reported that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder mutations in Nav1.7 increased resurgent sodium currents. They suggested that this may add to neuronal hyperexcitability.

checks.claim: Jarecki et al. (2010) reported that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder mutations in Nav1.7 increased resurgent sodium currents.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 7 cited papers. This 1959 paper does not cover Jarecki et al. (2010) or Nav1.7.

checks.claim: Jarecki et al. (2010) suggested that increased resurgent sodium currents from paroxysmal extreme pain disorder mutations in Nav1.7 may contribute to neuronal hyperexcitability.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 7 cited papers. This 1959 paper does not address Jarecki et al. (2010).

paragraphs.text: Some SCN9A mutations produce a mixed phenotype with features of both paroxysmal extreme pain disorder and erythromelalgia. Estacion et al. (2008) reported such an overlap with the A1632E mutation, which affected both activation and fast inactivation of the channel.

checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 4 cited papers. Only the title was supplied. It doesn't mention a mixed phenotype with erythromelalgia.

checks.claim: Estacion et al. (2008) reported an overlap phenotype of paroxysmal extreme pain disorder and erythromelalgia with the SCN9A A1632E mutation.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 7 cited papers. This 1959 paper does not address Estacion et al. (2008) or SCN9A.

checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 7 cited papers. This 1959 paper does not address Estacion et al. (2008) or how the channel behaves.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Episodic flushing, including harlequin color change

paragraphs.text: In a family with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, Fertleman et al. (2006) identified a heterozygous ile1461-to-thr (I1461T) mutation in the conserved inactivation gate motif of the domain III-IV linker of SCN9A. Functional studies showed that the mutant channel had impaired fast inactivation.
